clue.text: Ordered aaabcehillpt

indicators.note: ordered means put into an arrangement, so the string of letters that follows is rearranged into a word

explanation.surface: A jumble of lower-case letters described as being in order, like a filing instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed letters already sit in A-to-Z order, so the clue is both the fodder and its own definition: rearranged they spell the word that describes how they are printed.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters sorted from A to Z are in the order of the letter sequence, which is what this adjective describes.

clue.text: Self-confident young woman removing top on river north of Germany

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another comes above it
in a down clue, north of means placed above the next piece
taking off the top drops the first letter of the word for a young woman

parts.note: a lass is a young woman or girl
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, a crossword favourite
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: A confident girl stands by a river somewhere above Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' and 'north of' both mean coming before, so the pieces stack in the order given.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sure of themselves carries an assured manner; the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Pressure on poorly son to get these?

definitions.text: Pressure on poorly son to get these?

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another comes first

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
poorly is British for unwell, ill
S abbreviates son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Pressure is put on a sick boy to take his medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a poorly son is pushed to take tablets. 'Poorly' is everyday British for sick.
explanation.definitionFit: Tablets are what an ill child is pressed to swallow, which the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Adapts a cold area at an airport

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on taps
customs is the hall at an airport where luggage is checked for dutiable goods

explanation.surface: Someone adjusts to a chilly zone in an airport terminal.
explanation.definitionFit: To get someone used to new conditions is to adapt them; the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Utter age, upset

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone speaks of the passing years with dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like an adjective (complete) but is the verb, to give out a sound.
explanation.definitionFit: To utter a sound is to give it out or send it forth, a synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Naive person at home with no money

parts.note: to be in is to be at home
no cent means not a penny, no money at all

explanation.surface: A gullible stay-at-home who is broke.
explanation.definitionFit: A guileless, inexperienced person is called an innocent, a noun for someone unworldly.

clue.text: Long passage I will read out

indicators.note: something read out is spoken, so the clue words count for how they sound

parts.note: I will contracts to I'll

explanation.surface: Someone volunteers to recite a lengthy extract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long passage' suggests a stretch of text to read; it is a walkway between seats, as in a church or plane.
explanation.definitionFit: The walkway down a church nave or between rows of seats is a long, narrow corridor.

clue.text: Trade union initially leaving mother in the grip of bully

indicators.note: held in the grip of means enclosed, so one piece sits inside the bully word

parts.note: to bully someone into doing something is to coerce them

indicators.note: leaving signals that a letter departs from the mother word

parts.note: mum is British for mother

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of union

explanation.surface: A trade union boss abandons a mother caught by a bully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trade union' reads as one phrase, but 'Trade' alone is the definition; 'leaving' takes the union's first letter out of the mother word, and 'in the grip of' sets what remains inside the bully word.
explanation.definitionFit: Commerce is buying and selling on a large scale, the same sense as trade.

clue.text: Sunglasses suit husband rather than papa

indicators.note: rather than says one letter takes the place of another

parts.note: spades is one of the four suits in a pack of cards
Papa is P in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A man picks dark glasses to go with his suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' looks like clothing, but it is a card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Shades is informal for sunglasses, which shade the eyes.

clue.text: Pick lost niece out

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered here, so the letters of lost niece are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone chooses to search for a missing niece.
explanation.definitionFit: A pick is a choice, as in 'take your pick', the same as a choosing.

clue.text: Group interrupting quiet animal

indicators.note: breaking into a word, so the group word goes inside the quiet word

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
a lot is a group or batch, as at an auction

explanation.surface: A crowd disturbs a quiet creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The slow-moving tree-dwelling mammal of South America is a well-known example of an animal.

clue.text: Weather in Azores is terrific

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the words Azores is terrific

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker reports that the climate in the Azores is wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weather' looks like the noun of the surface but is the verb, to come through a storm.
explanation.definitionFit: To weather a storm is to withstand it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Second best editor cried

parts.note: the cream is the best part, as in the cream of the crop

explanation.surface: A runner-up editor wept at being second best.
explanation.definitionFit: To cry out loudly is to yell or shriek, the same as this verb.

clue.text: Physician flipping cross bandaging cut, lacking heart

indicators.note: bandaging wraps around, so the cut piece goes inside
flipping turns the word for a cross back to front

parts.note: a rood is a cross, as on a rood screen in a church

indicators.note: losing its heart drops the middle letter of cut

explanation.surface: An angry doctor dresses a wound that is missing its centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping cross' reads as a swearing, angry doctor; 'cross' is a rood, which turned round is DOOR, wrapped round CT.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor is a medical practitioner, which is what a physician is.

clue.text: Plant beginning to suffer after climate changes

indicators.note: one letter comes after the rearranged word
changes says the letters of climate shift into a new order
beginning to picks the first letter of suffer

explanation.surface: A garden plant starts to struggle when the climate shifts.
explanation.definitionFit: Clematis is a flowering climbing shrub grown in gardens, so an example of a plant.

clue.text: Prospective students might have to complete these costumes

definitions.text: Prospective students might have to complete these
definitions.meaning: read as two words, application forms for a university, which would-be students fill in
standard outfits worn by members of a group, such as school or police dress

explanation.surface: Would-be pupils must fill in paperwork for their outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as UNI FORMS for the first sense; 'uni' is British shorthand for university.
explanation.definitionFit: Identical outfits worn by a team, school or service are standard costumes.

clue.text: Overlooked foxtrot got tenor dancing

parts.note: Foxtrot is F in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: dancing moves the letters about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A singer was ignored when he danced the foxtrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foxtrot' and 'dancing' fit together as a ballroom picture, but foxtrot gives only F.
explanation.definitionFit: Something left out by mistake was neglected or not remembered, the same as being overlooked.

clue.text: Pleasant exercises with a climber

parts.note: sweet means pleasant or agreeable
PE is physical education, school exercises

explanation.surface: A nice workout with a mountaineer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climber' suggests a mountaineer; it is a climbing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet pea is a garden plant that climbs supports by tendrils, so a climber.

clue.text: Worries about saying cutting things

indicators.note: about means going round, so the worries word surrounds the saying

parts.note: to fret is to worry
a saw is an old saying or proverb

explanation.surface: Someone frets over a remark that hurts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting' suggests hurtful words; it means tools that cut.
explanation.definitionFit: These fine-bladed saws for intricate shapes in wood are tools that cut.

clue.text: One who doesn't eat more quickly

definitions.meaning: a person abstaining from food, as in a religious observance
the comparative of the adverb fast, at greater speed

explanation.definitionFit: Someone going without food observes a fast; the comparative of speedy is the second sense.

clue.text: Lawyer's underwear

definitions.meaning: a lawyer's cases, the instructions handed to a barrister

explanation.definitionFit: A barrister takes on cases called by this word, and short knickers or pants share the name.

clue.text: Please say it's wrong grabbing female

indicators.note: grabbing holds another piece inside
wrong signals that the letters of say it's are put into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone protests that it's an error to snatch a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges SAY IT'S into SATISY, and 'grabbing' puts F inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To please someone is to gratify or content them, a synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Salt is 50 per cent reduced with each diet, right?

indicators.note: cut by half, so only the second of the two letters of is remains

parts.note: fare is food, one's diet

explanation.surface: A dieter asks if halving salt in every meal is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' reads as table salt in a diet; an old salt is a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: An old salt is a veteran sailor, someone who travels the seas.

clue.text: A detective follows unknown old South American

indicators.note: the detective word comes after the unknown

parts.note: z is an unknown in algebra
tec is short for detective

explanation.surface: A sleuth trails a mysterious figure from long-ago South America.
explanation.walkthrough: The Aztecs were in fact in Mexico, usually called Central or North America; the setter stretches the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient empire of pre-conquest Mexico was ruled by this people, natives of the Americas.

clue.text: Looked for boozer that's disgusting inside

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the boozer word

parts.note: a sot is a drunkard, a boozer
ugh is the cry at something disgusting

explanation.surface: Someone hunted for a pub that is revolting within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boozer' looks like British slang for a pub; it is the drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of seek, which means to search or look for something.

clue.text: What dog might do to get bigger meal, finally?

parts.note: to grow is to get bigger

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of meal

explanation.surface: A dog might growl at its bowl to be given a larger dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog makes a low, threatening rumble in its throat, which is this verb.

clue.text: Food shop fine? Not half!

indicators.note: not half keeps only one half of the eight-letter word for fine, its front four letters

parts.note: delicate means fine, as in fine lace

explanation.surface: Someone asks if the grocer is fine and gets the British answer 'not half!' meaning very.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so'; here it means half of the word is lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for delicatessen, a shop selling cooked meats, cheeses and prepared foods.

clue.text: John almost backing writer

indicators.note: backing means the trimmed letters are read backwards
almost drops the last letter of the lavatory word

parts.note: john is slang for a lavatory

explanation.surface: A man called John nearly supports an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' looks like a man's name; it is the lavatory, giving TOILE when trimmed, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot and T. S. Eliot are both famous authors, examples of a writer.

clue.text: Ample bust upset Noel

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters of upset Noel are broken and reassembled

explanation.surface: Noel is upset about a large bust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' and 'upset' both look like anagram signals or a figure; 'bust' is the indicator and 'upset' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenteous means abundant or in good supply, the same as ample.

clue.text: Inspire friend from time to time

parts.note: to occasion something is to bring it about or prompt it
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Someone motivates a friend every so often.
explanation.definitionFit: Now and then, at irregular intervals, is the sense of this adverb.
